title: SHE DID NOT SCREAM. DOES THAT MEAN SHE CONSENTED? THE DISTURBING BIBLE PASSAGE WE NEED TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE WE JUDGE.
paragraphs: SHE DID NOT SCREAM. DOES THAT MEAN SHE CONSENTED? THE DISTURBING BIBLE PASSAGE WE NEED TO UNDERSTAND BEFORE WE JUDGE.
Deuteronomy 22:23–29, the ancient Hebrew context, the difference between coercion and consent, and the heart of a God who sees what human beings cannot.
Imagine being violated, traumatized, and terrified.
Then imagine standing before people who are supposed to defend you, only to hear them ask:
“Why didn't you scream?”
“Why didn't you fight back?”
“Why didn't you run?”
“Why did you stay silent?”
And perhaps the most devastating question of all…
“Are you sure you didn't want it?”
Sometimes, the wounds inflicted by the people who question a survivor become another source of suffering alongside the original violation.
Now imagine someone opening a Bible and using Scripture to justify that condemnation.
Suddenly, the wounded person is not only struggling with what happened to them. They are struggling with what they have been told about God.
Does God blame victims?
Does the Bible excuse sexual violence?
Did God really command a woman to marry the man who violated her?
These are not questions we should silence simply because they make us uncomfortable. They deserve careful, honest, compassionate, and biblically responsible answers.
Because when Scripture is taken out of context, the very words intended to guide humanity toward righteousness can be misused to deepen somebody's suffering.
Deuteronomy 22:23–29 is among the most controversial and frequently misunderstood passages in the Old Testament.

But before we condemn Scripture—or use it to condemn another human being—we must understand what the text actually says, the circumstances it addresses, and the ancient legal world in which it was written.
Deuteronomy 22:23–24 describes a situation involving a betrothed woman and a man who has sexual relations with her within a city.

In ancient Israel, betrothal was far more legally binding than modern engagement. A betrothed woman was already regarded as belonging to a legally established marital relationship, even before the marriage was fully consummated.
The passage treats this particular scenario as a violation of that relationship, assigning punishment to both parties and citing the woman's failure to cry out within the city.
The Hebrew word translated as crying out comes from צָעַק (tsa'aq), meaning to cry aloud, call for help, or appeal for deliverance.
Within this ancient legal scenario, the distinction between a populated city and an isolated field concerns the presumed availability of witnesses, assistance, and rescue.
But here is something we must understand.
Silence is not consent.

Modern knowledge of trauma recognizes that a person experiencing sexual violence may freeze, dissociate, become physically immobilized, or remain silent because of threats, fear, shock, or an involuntary survival response.
A person can desperately want to escape while being unable to move or speak.
The ancient legal presumption in this passage cannot responsibly be transformed into a universal test of whether someone consented.
The text presents a specific legal case. It does not explain every possible circumstance involving coercion, intimidation, trauma, or human behavior.
And no Christian should use this passage to declare that a survivor who could not scream must therefore have been willing.
Then the circumstances change.
Deuteronomy 22:25–26 says:
“But if a man find a betrothed damsel in the field, and the man force her, and lie with her: then the man only that lay with her shall die:
But unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing; there is in the damsel no sin worthy of death: for as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him, even so is this matter.”
— Deuteronomy 22:25–26, KJV
Read that again.
“Unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing.”
The Hebrew expression used in verse 25 is וְהֶחֱזִיק־בָּהּ (veheḥeziq-bah), derived from the root חָזַק (ḥazaq), which can convey strength, overpowering, or taking firm hold of someone.
In this context, it describes the man's forcible action against the woman.
The responsibility is placed upon the aggressor.
Not the woman.
Not her clothing.
Not her physical appearance.
Not her inability to escape.
Not her supposed failure to protect herself.
The text goes even further by comparing the offense to a man attacking and murdering his neighbor.
That comparison is extraordinary.
Sexual violence in this particular legal case is not treated as an innocent misunderstanding, a romantic mistake, or an unfortunate expression of uncontrollable desire.
It is treated as a grave act of violence.
Verse 27 explains that the woman cried out, but there was nobody to rescue her.
The Hebrew reads:
וְאֵין מוֹשִׁיעַ לָהּ
Ve'ein moshia la.
“And there was no one to save her.”
There is something heartbreaking about those ancient words.
No one came.
No one intervened.
No one was there to stop what was happening.
How many people today carry that same painful memory?
Perhaps it happened inside a house where they were supposed to feel safe.
Perhaps the person who harmed them was someone they trusted.
Perhaps they tried to tell somebody, but nobody believed them.
Perhaps they never found the courage to speak because they feared losing their family, their reputation, their marriage, their church community, or everything they had left.
And perhaps they are reading these words right now, wondering whether God sees them.
Hear this carefully.
Someone else's sin against you is not your sin.
Being violated does not make you spiritually unclean, morally worthless, or undeserving of love.
You are not responsible for another person's decision to harm you.
Your dignity was not theirs to take.
You were created in the image of God before the violation occurred, and you remain a person bearing that dignity afterward.
Genesis 1:27 has not stopped being true because somebody sinned against you.
But we must also confront the most difficult portion of this passage.
Deuteronomy 22:28–29.
“If a man find a damsel that is a virgin, which is not betrothed, and lay hold on her, and lie with her, and they be found;
Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days.”
— Deuteronomy 22:28–29, KJV
At first glance, the passage appears deeply disturbing.
Why would a man who violated a woman be required to marry her?
Would that not condemn her to a lifetime with the person who harmed her?
These are legitimate moral concerns, and Christians should not dismiss them with shallow explanations.
The Hebrew wording here differs from the wording in verse 25.
Instead of ḥazaq, verse 28 uses וּתְפָשָׂהּ (utefasah), from the Hebrew root תָּפַשׂ (taphas), meaning to seize, grasp, take hold of, or capture.

Some interpreters understand this distinction, together with the surrounding legal context, as indicating a different kind of sexual offense from the explicitly forcible assault described in verses 25–27.
Others understand verse 28 itself as describing sexual assault.
The Hebrew verb alone does not settle the question.
Taphas can describe forceful seizure, and the difference between the two Hebrew verbs cannot establish that the woman in verse 28 consented.
Verse 29 also uses עִנָּהּ (innah), from the Hebrew root עָנָה (anah), which in this verbal form can mean to afflict, humiliate, or violate.
The same root appears in other biblical accounts involving sexual violation, including the horrifying story of Tamar in 2 Samuel 13.
That is why intellectual honesty matters.
We cannot simply announce that the Hebrew proves this was consensual sex when the language does not establish that conclusion.
We must also consider Exodus 22:16–17, a related law concerning the seduction of an unbetrothed virgin.
In that passage, the Hebrew root פָּתָה (pathah) conveys enticing or persuading. The man is required to pay the customary marriage payment, but the woman's father can refuse the marriage.
Some interpreters read these passages together and argue that the refusal provision would also be relevant to Deuteronomy 22:28–29.
Others caution that the two laws describe different circumstances and that Deuteronomy does not explicitly repeat that provision.
Furthermore, neither passage expressly establishes the woman's independent right to refuse in the way modern understandings of consent would require.
We should acknowledge that limitation rather than pretending it does not exist.
In the ancient social and economic world, a woman's marital prospects could significantly affect her financial security, social standing, and future livelihood.

The requirement that the man pay compensation, assume continuing marital responsibility, and permanently surrender his right to divorce her can be understood as imposing obligations upon him rather than allowing him to walk away without consequences.
However, explaining that historical function does not eliminate every moral difficulty.
Nor does it mean that financial provision or marriage could erase the harm of sexual violence.
Marriage is not a cure for rape.
A wedding ceremony cannot transform coercion into consent.
A financial payment cannot purchase forgiveness.
And a woman should never be pressured to marry, remain with, or return to someone who sexually abuses her.
Understanding an ancient Israelite legal provision is not the same as commanding its direct application to every society throughout history.
The Bible itself contains a distinction between God's ultimate moral purposes and legal provisions addressing the broken realities of human society.
In Matthew 19:8, Jesus explains that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, while pointing back to God's original intention for marriage.

That passage is specifically about divorce, not Deuteronomy's sexual assault laws. Nevertheless, it demonstrates why Christians must carefully distinguish between particular Mosaic legal provisions and the fullness of God's moral purposes revealed through Christ.
Context matters.
Language matters.
Historical circumstances matter.
The difference between describing an ancient legal framework and prescribing modern Christian conduct matters.
And above all, the human being standing before us matters.
Think about Tamar.
In 2 Samuel 13, Amnon violates his own half-sister despite her explicit protests.
Afterward, he rejects her and sends her away.
Scripture does not romanticize his behavior.
It exposes his wickedness and records Tamar's devastation.
She tears her garment, places ashes upon her head, and goes away crying.
Her suffering is preserved within the pages of Scripture.
God's Word does not conceal the ugliness of what happened to her.
And yet, throughout history, how many modern Tamars have been told to remain silent to protect somebody else's reputation?
How many have been pressured to forgive immediately while the offender refuses to repent?
How many religious communities have protected influential people while abandoning those they harmed?
How many have confused keeping a scandal quiet with preserving the holiness of the Church?
But protecting a reputation at the expense of a wounded human being is not righteousness.
Concealing abuse is not grace.
Demanding silence is not reconciliation.
And forgiveness must never be manipulated into a demand that survivors abandon justice, accountability, safety, or appropriate legal action.
Jesus never taught us to protect wickedness in the name of mercy.
Ephesians 5:11 says:
“And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.”
The Gospel does not require us to pretend that evil never happened.
It brings darkness into the light.
It calls sinners to repentance.
It confronts hypocrisy.
It restores dignity.
It announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ without declaring that earthly consequences no longer matter.

A person who has committed sexual violence is not beyond the reach of God's grace, but genuine repentance cannot be reduced to tears, religious language, or an apology intended to escape accountability.
John the Baptist declared:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
— Matthew 3:8
Real repentance produces evidence of change.
It acknowledges wrongdoing without excuses.
It accepts responsibility.
It does not demand access to the person harmed.
It does not manipulate Scripture to escape consequences.
It does not confuse God's forgiveness with an entitlement to restored trust.
And for the wounded, the Gospel carries a different invitation.
Not an invitation to confess a sin committed against them.
Not an invitation to carry somebody else's shame.
But an invitation to encounter the Savior who draws near to the brokenhearted.
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
— Psalm 34:18
Jesus Christ knows what it means to suffer unjustly.
He knows betrayal.
He knows humiliation.
He knows what it means to endure violence at the hands of sinful humanity.
At Calvary, the innocent Son of God bore the judgment of sin so that through His death and resurrection, sinners could receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
The cross does not make evil insignificant.
It reveals both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable depth of divine love.
And the resurrection declares that suffering, darkness, and death do not have the final word.
That does not mean every wound disappears overnight.
Healing may involve years of prayer, professional trauma-informed care, safe relationships, medical assistance, and patient support.
Seeking such help is not a betrayal of faith.
You do not have to demonstrate your spirituality by suffering alone.
You do not have to publicly disclose your trauma to prove your courage.
You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you have forgiven.
And you do not have to pretend that everything is fine simply because you believe in Jesus.
Christ is not intimidated by the wounds you are still carrying.

Perhaps this article has challenged something you previously believed about Scripture. Perhaps it has reminded you of somebody whose pain was dismissed. Perhaps it has touched something you have never been able to put into words.
Or simply write, “Christ is still healing me.”
You do not owe the internet your personal story. Sometimes a few words are enough to remind another struggling soul that they are not alone.

This is why Gospel Warrior continues to create Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, discipleship materials, and resources that confront difficult realities while pointing people toward the transforming power of the Gospel.
Scripture teaches that those who benefit from spiritual instruction may support those who provide it (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
Not because God's love can be purchased.
But because generosity can be a meaningful expression of gratitude to God.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7
The Gospel is not a commodity.
Grace is not merchandise.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Deuteronomy 22:23–29 reminds us why we must approach Scripture with reverence, historical understanding, intellectual honesty, and compassion.
We must never twist the Bible to excuse an aggressor.
We must never manufacture linguistic arguments simply to avoid difficult questions.
We must never make wounded people carry the moral responsibility of those who harmed them.
And we must never forget that behind every theological discussion about sexual violence may be a human being silently reliving something we cannot imagine.
Let our churches become places where truth is spoken, abuse is confronted, the vulnerable are protected, repentance is genuine, and wounded people are treated with dignity.
Let our understanding of grace become deeper than religious slogans.
Let our commitment to justice become stronger than our desire to avoid scandal.
And let everything we do point toward Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel does not rewrite history by pretending the darkness never happened.
It rewrites our future by declaring that darkness does not have ultimate authority over those who belong to Christ.
Someone may have written a terrible chapter in your life, but they were never given the authority to write your ending.
